labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Auto-applied when the issue title/body matched no area label — needs maintainer review

items.body:
Child of #156. Implement an original KnowMe role pack for coordinator, memory curator, research, environment, artifact/integration, schedule/monitor, voice/meeting media, avatar/interpretation, outbound call and independent reviewer. Each definition needs actual system prompt, immutable ID/version/digest, input/output schema, exact tool/skill/resource allowlist, owner/tenant boundary, context lifecycle, per-task and team budgets, child scope and termination contract. Public definitions request capabilities; private DeploymentBinding/RepresentationGrant and an EffectiveBindingReceipt prove enforcement. No secret or human grant in public files.

Current-main evidence: BossFang `crates/librefang-types/src/agent.rs` supports native TOML prompts and coarse controls, but `crates/librefang-uar-spec/src/translator.rs` drops required budgets, context, owner, skills and stop semantics. UAR collaboration draft.2 is a document contract, not runtime conformance. Keep `kind: AgentDefinition`, publish a new versioned profile and fail closed on unsupported required fields, empty permissive allowlists or wildcard conversion. Parent authority is intersected into children; a media worker never gets connector write authority.

Acceptance: machine-readable definitions validate against a pinned schema and round-trip only where semantics are preserved; unsupported required fields reject activation. Two-owner, hostile-content, stale grant, budget exhaustion, cancellation and altered action tests prove no worker expands authority. Typed receipts and success predicates, not worker prose, finish the task. Respect original KBD #184/#185 and Mini #59 bounded phase exit. No OpenAI internal prompt claim.

items.title: Postgresql connector start is slow on multitenancy cases [DBZ-4840]
items.body:
Migrated from [DBZ-4840](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/DBZ-4840)

The postgresql connector is really slow to start up on my infrastructure (takes 17h).
For context, I'm using a postgresql DB with multitenancy (1 tenant = 1 schema), 4000 schemas and ~15 tables per schemas monitored.

Digging up, I found out it passed the most of that time [on this instruction|https://github.com/debezium/debezium/blob/6e581599c9e4261e446670332567dc1e6cd922c6/debezium-core/src/main/java/io/debezium/jdbc/JdbcConnection.java#L1201], a loop on every table to be snapshotted. On my connector, it was going at a speed of ~2 tables / seconds.

This behavior was introduced with DBZ-2575 (which does not improve performance when the number of tables to query is high), and can be set back to precedent using the parameter `database.internal.snapshot.scan.all.columns.force: true` (I spent way too long to find the needed prefix for this parameter). With this parameter set, this step now takes 5m on my infra (vs 17h).

Since this is an "internal" switch, I understand it isn't documented / might be changed at any moment. I'd suggest making this switch official and documented (e.g. on https://debezium.io/documentation/faq/, where there's already some good tips on handling large table numbers), and maybe send a log "info" if the number of tables to query is big (>600) with this parameter disabled as it can then takes a long time.

items.title: RFC: Add a preagg request type as an alternative to exec
items.body:
TL;DR before the proposal:
1. `exec` as currently constructed is too dangerous because it issues DML directly, which has two primary concerns
    1. DuckDB doesn't support serializing sql to json, which breaks the table allowlist
    2. Client schema/table naming is too much power. Our plan is to mount raw data in one schema per tenant as read-only, and have a separate writeable schema for materializations
2. Lost table definitions per #815 is intractable in the current design, if the coordinator remembers a table but it doesn't exist on the server. Reasons that underlying tables might get lost on the server
    1. Regular garbage collection: our plan is for preagg tables live ~24 hours
    2. Disk exhaustion: we might have to reap early if the disk is pressured
    3. Node recycle: running in the cloud, local SSDs are ephemeral, so if a node restarts, all preagg tables are eliminated
    4. WASM clearing: even running in the browser, some garbage collection may be necessary to prevent unbounded memory usage, or user clearing persistent data in the case of #651

To prevent having to fan out a DAG across all dependent tables, deterministic naming makes it possible to reconstitute underlying table definitions. That also has the benefit of multiple users in a tenant be able to share the same preagg tables if desired.

@jheer @domoritz I know this is long, but it isn't just slop for the sake of being long. I iterated over it and read through it several times

Client implementation in #1224 
- https://github.com/uwdata/mosaic/pull/1224

# Add a `preagg` request for authorized, recoverable preaggregation

## Proposal

Add `preagg`: the coordinator submits a SELECT, the server validates and materializes it, and the response supplies named `catalog`, `schema`, and `table` fields. The coordinator owns the recipe; the server owns physical storage and authorization. Add an explicit refresh option and an advisory `preagg_drop` cleanup hint.

[PreAggregator currently submits schema creation and CTAS through `exec`](https://github.com/uwdata/mosaic/blob/main/packages/mosaic/core/src/preagg/PreAggregator.ts). DuckDB's [`json_serialize_sql`](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/data/json/sql_to_and_from_json) supports SELECT serialization but not that creation DDL. The new operation lets restricted servers validate the source and construct the DDL themselves, while source catalogs remain read-only and arbitrary `exec` stays restricted.

This proposal covers preaggregate recovery and contributes an error contract to [#815](https://github.com/uwdata/mosaic/issues/815). Reloading missing source tables remains separate. The response also leaves room for [#389: Multi-tier Execution](https://github.com/uwdata/mosaic/issues/389).

## Wire contract

### Materialize or refresh

**`PreaggRequest`:**

```json
{
	"type": "preagg",
	"sql": "SELECT category, count(*) AS n FROM analytics.public.events GROUP BY category",
	"refresh": false
}
```

**`PreaggResponse`:**

```json
{
	"catalog": "memory",
	"schema": "mosaic_scope_a7",
	"table": "preagg_c92f",
	"createdAt": "2026-09-08T20:00:00Z"
}
```

| Field | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| Request `type` | Required literal `"preagg"`. |
| Request `sql` | Required nonempty string containing one supported SELECT statement. |
| Request `refresh` | Optional boolean, default `false`. `true` requires a new or shared in-progress build instead of reuse of a completed table. |
| Response `catalog`, `schema`, `table` | Required nonempty identifier strings assigned by the server. |
| Response `createdAt` | Required RFC 3339 timestamp of the successful build's completion. Reuse preserves it; rebuilding updates it. |

Success means a complete table is queryable. `createdAt` describes the build, not a source snapshot or an authorization grant. Validate the response before registering it; `{}` or malformed identifiers are errors.

Construct `new TableRefNode([catalog, schema, table])`, quoting each component separately. Mosaic's [internal array representation](https://github.com/uwdata/mosaic/blob/main/packages/mosaic/sql/src/ast/table-ref.ts) does not dictate the wire shape. A dotted string is not a substitute for the component array.

### Release a materialization

**`PreaggDropRequest`:**

```json
{
	"type": "preagg_drop",
	"catalog": "memory",
	"schema": "mosaic_scope_a7",
	"table": "preagg_c92f"
}
```

**`PreaggDropResponse`:**

```json
{
	"accepted": true
}
```

All request fields are required; the identifiers follow the response's component rules. No SQL is required. `accepted: true` acknowledges an authorized cleanup hint, without promising deletion. An authorized target already absent is a successful no-op.

### Transport and command decoding

Both operations use **HTTP POST or WebSocket messages only**; GET returns `bad_request`. Success is HTTP 200 JSON or one WebSocket JSON text message. Command validation becomes type-aware: `preagg` requires SQL; `preagg_drop` requires a target. Neither operation falls through to `exec`.

Keep application-owned payloads unrestricted; no metadata envelope is introduced. Protocol fields must be decoded independently of that payload.

## Identity, reuse, and freshness

**Unchanged definition, trusted scope, execution context, naming configuration, and optional host data revision produce the same fully qualified reference, including after eviction or restart.** Mosaic uses the returned name rather than computing it.

```text
table_name = "preagg_" + SHA256(encode(
	"preagg-v1", trusted_scope, execution_context, data_revision, exact_select_sql
))
```

Use unambiguous encoding. Scope includes any user-specific grants or row restrictions that affect sharing; execution context includes bindings or settings that change the SQL's meaning. These values come from trusted host decisions. The examples abbreviate hashes; full SHA-256 hex plus `preagg_` is 71 characters. Shortened names require full-digest collision checks, and a collision must never reuse another definition.

Hash exact snapshotted SQL: whitespace and alias changes can create duplicate tables. Hashing a serialized AST is an alternative, but serializer upgrades can rename tables. Store the full definition digest, relevant context, and build timestamp in server-controlled metadata tied to the table; a table comment can aid inspection. Verify this metadata on reuse. A matching name alone is insufficient.

| Situation | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Coordinator forgot; authorized reusable table remains | A new `preagg` reattaches and registers the recipe again. No server recipe cache is required. |
| Server lost a table; coordinator retained the recipe | Resubmit the SELECT and rebuild at the same reference while naming inputs are unchanged. |
| Data changed and the application requests refresh | Send `refresh: true`, rebuild, invalidate affected result caches, and resume dependent queries after success. |
| Host revision or destination configuration changes | The response may identify a new table; regenerate managed builder queries using that reference. |

**Refresh is a real operation.** Under the same naming inputs, build and replace the table transactionally at the existing reference. Concurrent refreshes can share one in-progress build. Failure must leave no partial replacement and must not report the old table as refreshed. A retained old table may remain available to other readers, but the requesting coordinator falls back rather than treating it as fresh.

Starting refresh advances the local recipe generation and invalidates dependent caches; earlier results cannot repopulate them or update views. Server query-result caches must include the build generation or be invalidated on replacement, even when the table name stays the same.

Hosts may incorporate a source revision into naming instead of replacing a prior revision's table. Such a revision must correspond to the inputs actually read, using pinned snapshots or an equivalent consistency check. Applications must notify the coordinator when data changes and request refresh; hashing and `createdAt` do not detect source updates. Other coordinators and their caches need the same invalidation signal if they must observe that update.

**Configuration changes:** Catalog, schema, or naming changes may require new bindings and regenerated dependent SQL. Raw SQL embedding an old reference requires a caller update. Old tables may need separate cleanup. Authentication or connector changes reset the affected coordinator state entirely.

## Coordinator lifecycle and query construction

### Proposed API

| API | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `Connector.query(PreaggRequest)` | `Promise<PreaggResponse>`. |
| `Connector.query(PreaggDropRequest)` | `Promise<PreaggDropResponse>`. |
| `Coordinator.preagg(query: SelectQuery \| string, options?: { refresh?: boolean })` | `QueryResult<TableRefNode>`, backed by a retained recipe. |
| `Coordinator.forgetPreagg(table: TableRefNode)` | `void`; retire the recipe and dependent work, and schedule a release hint. |

```javascript
const mc = new Coordinator(readConnector, {
	preagg: { enabled: true, mode: 'preagg', connector: materializationConnector }
});

const sql = 'SELECT category, count(*) AS n FROM analytics.public.events GROUP BY category';
const table = await mc.preagg(sql);
await mc.query(Query.from(table).select('*'));

// Application data-refresh event:
const refreshed = await mc.preagg(sql, { refresh: true });
await mc.query(Query.from(refreshed).select('*'));
```

### Recipes outlive `PreAggregator.entries`

Maintain a coordinator-owned registry indexed by exact SELECT text and returned reference within the current connector and authorization context. Store the SQL snapshot, current binding, build metadata, pending build, generation, and dependent query templates. Ordinary repeated registration shares a pending build or reuses a ready entry without another network request. Explicit refresh bypasses that shortcut.

`PreAggregator.clear()` only clears client-to-info mappings and invalidates obsolete selection work. It must not retire recipes or emit drop hints on every `requestQuery()` or active-source change. Zero currently attached consumers can leave a reusable idle recipe.

Consumers are live `PreAggregateInfo` objects and explicit `Coordinator.preagg()` registrations. `forgetPreagg()` explicitly retires the logical recipe; disabling automatic preaggregation retires automatic-only recipes, while explicit registrations remain until forgotten. Connector or authorization-context changes retire all affected recipes and caches. These lifecycle events, not ordinary selection clearing, schedule release hints. Generation checks prevent late responses from reviving retired state.

### Wait before constructing dependent SQL

Snapshot `create.toString()` when requesting materialization. Cache a pending `PreAggregateInfo` immediately so repeated requests share it. In the new mode, `table` and `select` are nullable until `ready: Promise<TableRefNode>` resolves; finalize `select` with the returned table then. `updateSelection` awaits readiness, checks that its selection generation is still current, and only then calls `info.query(active)`.

This preserves the existing fallback to a normal query when creation or use fails. Timeout and resource failures reject the current attempt but do not permanently poison the recipe; a later interaction or explicit retry can try again with backoff. No mutable `TableRefNode` is required: retain query templates and construct new nodes when a binding changes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
	participant C as Coordinator
	participant S as Materialization connector / server
	participant D as DuckDB
	C->>C: Snapshot SELECT and share pending recipe
	C->>S: preagg SELECT, optional refresh
	S->>S: Authorize and derive reference
	alt Reuse allowed
		S->>S: Verify completed table and definition
	else Build or refresh
		S->>D: Coalesced transactional materialization
		D-->>S: Complete table committed
	end
	S-->>C: Reference and createdAt
	C->>C: Resolve ready and finalize dependent SQL
	C->>S: SELECT from returned reference
```

## Scheduling and limits

`preagg` is synchronous and bounded by a server command deadline, including each WebSocket message. Connector closure and transport timeouts must settle active requests rather than leave `ready` pending indefinitely. It can occupy a SQL-pool connection for its duration. Servers need a separate materialization concurrency cap and admission budget so builds do not consume all read capacity.

Use a separate coordinator scheduling lane for both new commands: bypass SQL-result caching, Arrow consolidation, and ordered `pendingResults` delivery; do not set `pendingExec`. Dependent queries wait on their recipe, while independent queries can complete. Explicit data-loading dependencies must still be awaited. This also prevents a `preagg` response from entering the SQL-only cache under the same key as an Arrow query. The current queue behavior is in [QueryManager](https://github.com/uwdata/mosaic/blob/main/packages/mosaic/core/src/QueryManager.ts).

Add optional `preagg.connector` for this lane, defaulting to the main connector. Use REST or a dedicated socket when the primary connector is a [single-request WebSocket](https://github.com/uwdata/mosaic/blob/main/packages/mosaic/core/src/connectors/socket.ts); sharing that socket still serializes requests despite separate coordinator scheduling. Both connectors must reach compatible database state and the same authorization context. Proxy timeouts still apply.

Servers enforce per-materialization row/byte limits, per-scope quotas, total memory and spill budgets, and maximum duration. Reserve capacity before admission and remove incomplete/over-limit outputs. Expose host eviction hooks, such as LRU within a scope. Client cardinality controls, such as [#1071](https://github.com/uwdata/mosaic/issues/1071), complement these server limits.

## Server validation and publication

### A supported SELECT is precisely defined

For the DuckDB implementation, require successful serialization of exactly one statement with a query root of `SELECT_NODE`, `SET_OPERATION_NODE`, `RECURSIVE_CTE_NODE`, or `CTE_NODE`. This includes VALUES, set operations, and supported CTEs. Reject `SHOW_REF` anywhere, unresolved `PARAMETER` nodes, unsupported roots, and additional statements; successful serialization alone does not establish safety.

Run the same configured source, function, and external-access policies as for Arrow queries, plus application validators. Resolve CTEs in their lexical scope. Every physical `BASE_TABLE` must resolve to an authorized source; a path disguised as a table name or an unapproved replacement scan cannot bypass policy. Macros and table functions must also satisfy host policy. Bind validation and execution to the same authorized context and exact SQL snapshot.

### Authorize derived data, not just its namespace

- Derive destination scope on the server, create its schema as needed, and construct DDL using safely quoted identifiers. Drop requests must match an authorized server-managed target; echoing a name grants no rights.
- Authorize every read, reuse, and rebuild. Source revocation needs either retained dependency metadata checked on reads, or an authorization-policy epoch that makes old references and cached results inaccessible. Scope ownership alone does not prevent access to data derived from a revoked source. Physical cleanup can follow logical revocation.
- Match sharing scope to effective permissions, including row restrictions. Dependency metadata and ownership must remain verifiable for as long as their tables survive; metadata loss cannot silently allow reuse.

### Publish once, after completion

The server **must coalesce concurrent builds per fully qualified reference**, after authorizing each requester. Coalesce initial schema creation per namespace as well. Use transactional CTAS/replacement and publish the table and its metadata only after successful completion. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` alone is not concurrency control. If another writer wins a creation race, wait within the deadline, then verify the completed object's definition before reuse; never blindly retry an unverified conflict or cache a failed build as existing.

Use ordinary tables in an in-memory catalog or other host-managed storage. DuckDB [temporary tables](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/sql/statements/create_table#temporary-tables) are connection-scoped and are unsuitable across the Go server's separate SQL and Arrow pools. Identical names do not share process-local storage: hosts need request affinity, shared storage, or accepted rebuilds across replicas.

## Recovery and error contract

### Structured errors across transports

Supporting servers return JSON command errors over HTTP and WebSocket, including errors from subsequent SELECTs. REST and socket connectors preserve `code` and reference fields; legacy plain-text errors remain generic failures.

```json
{
	"error": "Materialized table is unavailable",
	"code": "table_not_found",
	"catalog": "memory",
	"schema": "mosaic_scope_a7",
	"table": "preagg_c92f"
}
```

| Code | HTTP status | Coordinator behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `table_not_found` | 404 | Recover only a matching live preaggregate recipe. |
| `deadline_exceeded` | 504 | End this attempt; automatic preaggregation may use an authorized base query. |
| `resource_exhausted` | 429 | Same fallback; suppress immediate repeated builds. |
| `forbidden` / `unauthenticated` | 403 / 401 | Do not rebuild or bypass the authorization failure. |
| `bad_request` | 400 | Surface invalid input; no automatic rebuild. |
| `unsupported_command` | 400 | Surface unsupported deployment/mode; never fall back to `exec`. |
| `internal_error` | 500 | Surface failure; no unbounded recovery. |

Classify missing managed relations structurally. After scope-aware AST authorization, resolve their references against the catalog, for example using host-owned `duckdb_tables()` queries. Missing managed catalogs or schemas count too. Coordinate this check with eviction through execution, or recheck structural existence after an execution failure. Do not infer identities by parsing DuckDB error strings. Include a reference only after establishing that it belongs to the caller's managed namespace; never echo arbitrary forbidden targets as recovery instructions.

### The coordinator owns recovery

The recipe registry survives a server restart while the coordinator remains alive. A page reload requires application recreation or persistence. Servers may retain recipes and rebuild transparently, but the protocol works without that cache; a stored name alone is not a recipe.

Map failures through `PreAggregateInfo`, matching registered `TableRefNode`s in builder ASTs, or the structured error reference for raw SQL. Remove the rejected promise's exact query-cache key before retrying. Keep logical recipe identity separate from its current physical reference.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
	participant C as Coordinator
	participant S as Server
	C->>S: SELECT using a registered table
	S-->>C: table_not_found with authorized reference
	C->>C: Match live recipe and share one recovery attempt
	C->>S: preagg with retained SELECT
	S-->>C: Authorized table reference
	alt Same reference
		C->>S: Retry original SELECT once
	else Reference changed
		C->>C: Rebind recipe and invalidate affected caches
		C->>C: Regenerate managed builder queries
		C->>S: Retry regenerated SELECT once
	end
```

Reference changes are recoverable for coordinator-managed builder queries: rebuild their templates with the new reference, track the old-to-current binding within that recipe, and invalidate dependent caches and queued generations. Cloning and consolidation must retain the originating logical requests so they can be regenerated before serialization. Do not text-replace SQL or mutate arbitrary user queries. Raw SQL can retry unchanged when the reference stays the same; otherwise surface the changed reference for the caller to rebuild its SQL.

Allow one rebuild per reference per failure epoch and one SELECT retry within the operation's deadline; concurrent misses share the attempt. Server-transparent recovery follows the same bound and must preserve the reference used by the incoming SQL. Cancellation, forgetting, permission errors, and failed rebuilds cannot cause retry loops. Missing source tables and recursive recipe dependencies remain #815 work.

## Release semantics

`forgetPreagg()` completes locally without waiting for `preagg_drop`; log transport failures without restoring forgotten state. The server may retain, defer, or reap an authorized target. Drop is neither a freshness operation nor a distributed reference count.

Other coordinators may still use the same table, and an old hint can arrive after re-registration. Reaping must consult current activity and coordinate with builds and running queries; hosts may safely ignore all hints initially. Later queries use recovery or an authorized fallback if a table was reaped. A later explicit `preagg` can reuse any retained table.

## Compatibility and initial scope

Keep `preagg.mode: 'exec' | 'preagg'`, initially defaulting to `'exec'`. `preagg.enabled` controls automatic preaggregation; direct `Coordinator.preagg()` always uses the new operation. In the new mode, `preagg.schema` assignments warn and do nothing, including the widget's `preagg_schema` traitlet, so initialization does not throw or select a server destination. However, `dropSchema()` rejects with `unsupported_command` and guidance to refresh or release recipes; a successful no-op could incorrectly signal that stale data was invalidated.

| Component | Support requirement |
| --- | --- |
| REST / Socket connectors and Go server | Initial reference implementation of commands, structured errors, scheduling, and managed-reference authorization. |
| Local Wasm / Node connectors | Implement local materialization handlers returning real catalog/schema/table identifiers before enabling the mode; known unsupported connectors must reject mode selection. |
| Python / Rust servers and Jupyter transport | After the design is proved and settled in the Go implementation, add to other servers |

Legacy servers currently return differing unknown-command errors; those are not successful materializations. Remote support may only be learned on the first request. Preserve explicit unsupported errors and reject malformed responses instead of treating every generic HTTP 400/500 as `unsupported_command`. No automatic capability negotiation is required initially.

Ship creation/refresh/drop, recipe lifetime, asynchronous integration, and bounded preaggregate recovery together so the new mode does not depend on arbitrary `exec` or permanent tables. Broader source recovery remains separate.

Validate the following before enabling the mode:

- SELECT-root, CTE, parameter, replacement-scan, function, URI, and scope rejection; GET rejection and type-aware decoding.
- Fully qualified quoting across transports/pools; narrow catalog authorization; source revocation and isolation between effective scopes.
- Concurrent create/refresh conflicts, atomic publication, quota failures, timeouts, independent-query completion, and safe retry backoff.
- Registry survival across ordinary `clear()`; connector/scope reset, explicit registrations, retirement, and late responses.
- Refresh with unchanged and changed references; builder cloning/consolidation, raw-SQL limits, stale result-cache invalidation, and SQL-cache isolation from Arrow requests.
- Restart without server recipes, missing managed catalog/schema/table, shared rebuilds, lost inputs, and bounded failed recovery.
- Duplicate/delayed release hints and cross-coordinator reuse; legacy mode and widget compatibility.

## Future Work

### Return small preaggregates for local execution — #389

A future transfer hint could be `maxInlineBytes`:

```json
{
	"type": "preagg",
	"sql": "SELECT category, count(*) AS n FROM analytics.public.events GROUP BY category",
	"maxInlineBytes": 5000000
}
```

Still materialize on the server and always return the remote reference. If the complete table fits the threshold, optionally return it for a client query engine such as DuckDB-Wasm. A partial table must never count as a complete cache. Define the threshold using encoded transfer bytes, with a separate client memory budget after decoding.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
	A[Materialize on server] --> B{Complete table fits transfer hint?}
	B -->|Yes, and supported| C[Return remote reference and whole table]
	B -->|No| D[Return remote reference]
	C --> E[Coordinator tracks local and remote bindings]
	E --> F[Eligible queries run locally]
	E --> G[Remote fallback after local eviction]
	D --> G
```

Keep the remote binding, recipe, and build metadata separate from the local binding. Both caches follow refresh and authorization changes. Mixed local/remote joins and planning remain #389 work. JSON identifiers plus Arrow data require explicit framing: for WebSocket, define either a correlated JSON/binary message pair or metadata inside the binary stream before supporting combined responses.

### Longer builds and lifecycle hints

An asynchronous operation returning `status: "pending"` with polling or server push could avoid long command waits. TTL hints such as `ttlMs`, guaranteed leases/deletion, source-revision wire fields, and client-side transfer remain outside the initial contract.

items.title: PostgreSQL connector: WARN spam from TypeRegistry in multi-schema deployments
items.body:
## Bug report

**What Debezium connector do you use and what version?**

`io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector`, version `3.4.3.Final` (also reproduced on `3.5.0.Final`)

---

**What is the connector configuration?**

```json
{
  "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
  "plugin.name": "pgoutput",
  "publication.autocreate.mode": "disabled",
  "publication.name": "cdc",
  "table.include.list": ".+\\.(table_a|table_b|table_c|table_d|...)$",
  "tasks.max": "1",
  "snapshot.mode": "no_data",
  "heartbeat.interval.ms": "5000"
}
```

Note: no `schema.include.list` — we capture from all tenant schemas by design.

---

**What is the captured database version and mode of deployment?**

Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, managed (AWS RDS), MSK Connect.

---

**What behavior do you expect?**

The "Type is already mapped" condition should not log at WARN level when the duplicate is simply a same-named type in a different schema. This is expected in any multi-tenant or multi-schema PostgreSQL deployment and is not indicative of a problem.

---

**What behavior do you see?**

~17,000 WARN-level log lines per connector startup:

```
WARN  Type [oid:278431, name:accounts] is already mapped   [io.debezium.connector.postgresql.TypeRegistry]
WARN  Type [oid:278432, name:users] is already mapped       [io.debezium.connector.postgresql.TypeRegistry]
WARN  Type [oid:278433, name:enrollments] is already mapped [io.debezium.connector.postgresql.TypeRegistry]
... (repeated for every type × every tenant schema)
```

On MSK Connect, there is no per-class log level configuration, so we cannot suppress these via logging config. The volume drowns out genuine warnings from the connector.

---

**Do you see the same behaviour using the latest released Debezium version?**

Yes — the `addType()` method is unchanged in `3.5.0.Final`. Not verified against any Alpha/Beta/CR builds, but the code path has not changed on `main`.

---

**Do you have the connector logs, ideally from start till finish?**

The relevant logs are the WARN lines themselves — samples are shown above.

---

**How to reproduce the issue using our [[tutorial](https://github.com/debezium/debezium-examples/tree/main/tutorial)](https://github.com/debezium/debezium-examples/tree/main/tutorial) deployment?**

1. Create a PostgreSQL database with multiple schemas sharing the same table definitions:

```sql
CREATE SCHEMA tenant_1;
CREATE SCHEMA tenant_2;
CREATE SCHEMA tenant_3;
-- repeat for N schemas

CREATE TABLE tenant_1.table_a (id bigint primary key, name text);
CREATE TABLE tenant_2.table_a (id bigint primary key, name text);
CREATE TABLE tenant_3.table_a (id bigint primary key, name text);
-- repeat for each schema
```

2. Configure the connector with `table.include.list` matching all schemas (no `schema.include.list`):

```json
{
  "table.include.list": ".+\\.table_a$"
}
```

3. Start the connector. Observe WARN lines for every `table_a` composite type after the first schema.

The number of warnings scales as `(num_schemas - 1) × num_types_per_schema`.

---

### Cause

In [`[TypeRegistry.addType()](https://github.com/debezium/debezium/blob/v3.5.0.Final/debezium-connector-postgres/src/main/java/io/debezium/connector/postgresql/TypeRegistry.java#L143-L147)`](https://github.com/debezium/debezium/blob/v3.5.0.Final/debezium-connector-postgres/src/main/java/io/debezium/connector/postgresql/TypeRegistry.java#L143-L147), the `nameToType` map is keyed solely by type name:

```java
if (!nameToType.containsKey(type.getName())) {
    nameToType.put(type.getName(), type);
}
else {
    LOGGER.warn("Type [oid:{}, name:{}] is already mapped", type.getOid(), type.getName());
}
```

The underlying `SQL_TYPES` query joins `pg_namespace` but the namespace is never propagated into the map key. When schema `tenant_1` and schema `tenant_2` both define a composite type `accounts`, the second one triggers a WARN.

In our environment (Canvas LMS — a multi-tenant PostgreSQL application), a single database has hundreds of schemas sharing identical table/type definitions. This produces **~17,000 WARN lines per connector startup**, repeated on every restart or rebalance.

### Why existing fixes don't help

- **PR #7150 (schema-filtered type loading)**: Filters `pg_type` to `schema.include.list` schemas. Our connector captures tables from _all_ schemas (`table.include.list: ".+\\.(table_names...)$"`) — we have no `schema.include.list` because every tenant schema is needed. Even if we enumerated all schemas, the duplicates across them would still trigger warnings.
- **DBZ-5182 (ascending OID order)**: Addressed type _collisions_ from extension schemas overriding built-in types, but did not change the log level or namespace handling.
- **#1683 / #1800 (performance fixes)**: Reduced startup time from OID lookups and double initialization, but the WARN-level logging remains.

### Relationship to [DBZ-8519](https://github.com/debezium/dbz/issues/1323)

[DBZ-8519](https://github.com/debezium/dbz/issues/1323) reports the same symptom but from a different angle — the reporter has many schemas and expected `schema.include.list` to suppress the warnings. Our case is distinct: we intentionally capture all schemas, so schema filtering is not a viable workaround. The underlying code issue (name-only keying, WARN log level) is the same.

### Suggested fix

Downgrade the log level from `LOGGER.warn` to `LOGGER.debug` in `TypeRegistry.addType()`. The "already mapped" condition is a normal consequence of PostgreSQL's type system when multiple schemas define same-named types. It is not a correctness issue — the first-registered type wins, and `oidToType` still maps every OID correctly. The `nameToType` map is used for well-known type name lookups (e.g., `hstore`, `geometry`) that don't carry schema context, so the first-wins behavior is the right semantics here.
